title: Conflict patterns across Myanmar townships
text:
Where do recorded armed-conflict events and reported fatalities cluster across Myanmar townships, and how did local concentrations evolve between January 2021 and September 2025?
The analysis distinguishes absolute burden, spatial association, and temporal change in clustering. A large count does not by itself establish a statistically significant hotspot. A hotspot does not establish why violence occurred. The intended use is retrospective peace-building and humanitarian situational awareness at township level, not targeting, tactical planning, or individual risk prediction.
This report follows the Take-home Exercise 2 brief. The companion executive summary presents the central findings. All outputs below derive from the supplied data rather than textbook example numbers.

2.1 Sources and variables








Input

Township boundaries obtained through MIMU GeoNode
330 unique township P-codes; embedded PCode_V is 9.4



The CSV contains violent and non-violent event types. The primary operational definition retains Battles, Explosions/Remote violence, and Violence against civilians within Myanmar. Protests, riots and strategic developments are excluded. This is an armed-conflict subset, not every event in ACLED’s broader political-violence category. The latter can include specific protest and riot subtypes. See the ACLED Codebook.
Two outcomes are analysed: the number of retained records and the sum of their reported fatalities. Fatalities represent recorded estimates, not an independently verified death toll. No population denominator is supplied, so neither outcome estimates per-capita risk. A zero bin means no retained record in this extract; it does not prove the absence of violence or complete reporting.
The boundary download request is preserved in data/Geospatial/wfsrequest.txt. The local file confirms the required version through its attributes. The source does not independently establish that every boundary reflects conditions in every study month. No download date is inferred from a file modification timestamp.
The course brief identifies eLearn as the distribution channel for its ACLED dataset. This report records the supplied filename and input fingerprint, but the local CSV alone does not verify its acquisition channel or download date. These provenance details require the original download record. The three retained event categories operationalise armed conflict consistently throughout the analysis.

4.1 Global context and Moran scatterplots
This supplementary step adapts the Global Moran’s I workflow in Hands-on Exercise 5(1) and the centred scatterplot in Hands-on Exercise 5(2), based on the course’s Chapter 9 and Chapter 10. Hunan GDPPC is replaced by the two Myanmar township totals. The existing queen-based graph, isolate repairs, township order and row standardisation are retained; the focal township is excluded.
The null randomly reallocates the observed totals across the fixed national graph. Each outcome uses 9,999 permutations and a fixed seed, with the null statistics generated by moran.mc. To avoid a zero simulated p-value, the reported two-sided p is twice the smaller inclusive tail probability, capped at one; each tail is (1 + number of equally or more extreme simulations) / 10,000. This explicit finite-simulation convention replaces the function’s returned p-value. Holm adjustment covers these two global tests only, separately from the existing local BH families. Under random allocation the expected I is -1/329, not exactly zero. This is a supplementary overall check, not a prerequisite for local analysis or a replacement for EHSA.


Show code
global_table <- global_moran$results %>%
  transmute(Outcome=ifelse(variable=='events','Event counts','Reported fatalities'),
            `Moran I`=round(I,4),`Null expectation`=round(null_expectation,4),
            `Permutation p`=sprintf('%.4f',permutation_p),
            `Holm p (2 tests)`=sprintf('%.4f',holm_p),Permutations=permutations)
kable(global_table)

Both outcomes show positive overall spatial association at the two-test Holm 0.05 threshold. The larger fatality I does not establish a statistically tested difference between outcomes. Population, reporting coverage and other spatial heterogeneity can violate the national exchangeability assumption; these are count-based associations, not per-capita risks or causal effects.






Figure 4: Moran scatterplots for both outcomes, using the same weights and totals as the existing local analysis.



Each point is a township. The axes show its standardised total and the neighbour average of the same standardised variable. The line through the origin has slope I because the weights sum to 330. Colours distinguish descriptive quadrants; triangles identify existing local Moran BH q < 0.05 results. Quadrant membership alone does not establish significance. Both panels use the same axis scales and raw totals before standardisation.

4.1.1 Sensitivity to skewness and spatial weights
For each outcome, a two-by-two comparison crosses raw totals and log1p(total) with the original queen graph and a symmetric six-nearest-neighbour graph. The latter uses the same projected representative points as the existing local sensitivity analysis. Symmetrisation retains an edge selected by either township, so final degrees can exceed six. All graphs exclude self-neighbours and use row-standardised weights. The transformation retains zeros and reduces the influence of large totals, but changes the measured variable and does not adjust for population or reporting.
Each setting uses 9,999 permutations and the same outcome-specific seed. Holm adjustment jointly covers all eight outcome/setting tests, including the two original raw/queen tests. The earlier two-test adjusted values remain labelled separately; none is substituted into local or EHSA results.

title: Conflict patterns across Myanmar townships
text:
5.1 Event counts






Figure 5: Local Moran’s I for event totals.



At unadjusted p < 0.05, 37 townships form High-High clusters, 50 Low-Low clusters, 0 High-Low outliers and 2 Low-High outliers. High-High examples include Hpa-An (Kayin); Myawaddy (Kayin); Kyainseikgyi (Kayin). These categories compare a township with its neighbours, not with its own past. Low-Low clusters may reflect low recorded activity or weaker observation; they do not establish safety.






Figure 6: Gi* for event totals.



The Gi* test identifies 38 hot-spot and 52 cold-spot townships at p < 0.05. It measures local concentrations including the focal area, whereas Moran’s I distinguishes clusters from outliers. These two maps therefore answer related but different questions. A significant hotspot supports unusually high local recorded burden under this reference model, not an explanation of its causes. The largest regional concentration is Sagaing, containing 17 of these nominal event-count hot spots.

title: Conflict patterns across Myanmar townships
text:
5.2 Reported fatalities






Figure 7: Local Moran’s I for reported fatalities.



Reported fatalities produce 38 High-High clusters and 0 High-Low outliers at p < 0.05. High-High examples include Kyainseikgyi (Kayin); Falam (Chin); Hakha (Chin). Fatality-based association need not reproduce event-count association: a small number of severe incidents can strongly affect the sum. Uncertain fatality reporting and differences in incident severity are therefore central limitations.






Figure 8: Gi* for reported fatalities.



The fatality Gi* test yields 43 hot-spot and 66 cold-spot townships. 33 townships are nominal hot spots under both outcomes. Agreement supports reviewing those areas across both frequency and recorded severity, but neither measure provides a population-adjusted estimate or an independently verified death toll. Sagaing contains the largest number: 22 nominal fatality hot spots.

title: Conflict patterns across Myanmar townships
text:
6.1 Space-time neighbourhood and classification
For each township-month, the Gi* neighbourhood contains the focal township and its spatial neighbours in the current month and the preceding month. January 2021 has no earlier bin and uses its current-month neighbourhood only. This is a retrospective, one-lag specification, not a forecasting model. Row standardisation accounts for differing neighbourhood sizes. The reference is the complete study cube, so national temporal change can contribute to local trends.
Space-time Gi* uses 999 conditional permutations with the focal observation fixed. A compiled Rcpp helper samples distinct non-focal bins by rejection sampling, avoiding full-population shuffles for every sparse neighbourhood. The two-sided p-value is twice the smaller inclusive-tail count, with a plus-one correction, capped at one. This handles ties conservatively. The helper was checked against exhaustive enumeration on a small graph; its Gi* z-values are computed by spdep::localG. Significant positive and negative bins define hot and cold episodes. A Mann-Kendall test of each township’s 57 Gi* z-values measures monotonic change in clustering strength. Its tau is an ordinal association, not an events-per-month growth rate.
Sign-specific rules distinguish new, consecutive, intensifying, diminishing, persistent, historical, sporadic and oscillating patterns. For persistent/intensifying/diminishing patterns, at least 90% of bins must be significant in the same direction. The classification uses the versioned ArcGIS Pro 3.4 pattern definitions, implemented explicitly in R. In particular, a sporadic hot or cold spot must be significant in the same direction in September 2025, have an earlier same-sign episode, fewer than 90% same-sign bins, and no opposite-sign episode. Earlier intermittent episodes with a non-significant final bin do not qualify. This definition differs from older documentation that omitted the terminal requirement.
The R workflow follows these pattern definitions but uses its own permutation-based inference. It does not reproduce ArcGIS numerically. The primary maps use nominal bin p-values to make the exercise’s p < 0.05 threshold explicit. A separate sensitivity analysis classifies BH-adjusted bins, because the documented ArcGIS workflow uses multiple-testing correction. The two inference conventions must not be conflated.
The map additionally requires Mann-Kendall p < 0.05 and a recognised pattern. A persistent hotspot without a significant trend can therefore be present in the full results but grey on this significance-filtered map. That is an intentional distinction between persistent clustering and evidence of change.






Figure 9: Space-time Gi* trajectories for high-burden townships.



The heatmap contrasts clustering strength through time for the twenty highest-count townships. Its colours show z-values rather than a significance mask. It helps distinguish sustained concentrations from brief episodes before looking at the final classifications. Selection by total burden means this view is illustrative rather than representative of all townships.

title: Conflict patterns across Myanmar townships
text:
6.2 Event-count patterns






Figure 10: Event-count EHSA, filtered by significant Mann-Kendall trends.



220 townships meet the unadjusted Mann-Kendall threshold; 60 also have a recognised EHSA pattern and appear in colour. Positive tau indicates increasing Gi* values, which can mean intensifying high-value clustering or weakening low-value clustering. Negative tau has the reverse interpretation. The class label and the sign of Gi* must therefore be read together.

title: Conflict patterns across Myanmar townships
text:
6.3 Fatality patterns






Figure 11: Fatality EHSA, filtered by significant Mann-Kendall trends.



220 townships meet the Mann-Kendall threshold for reported fatalities, of which 58 also have a recognised pattern. This map assesses changes in the spatial concentration of recorded fatalities. It does not estimate changes in casualty risk, and sharp episodes can influence the Gi* trajectory even when the broader pattern is not monotonic.

New patterns appear only in the final significant bin. Consecutive patterns form a single terminal run of at least two months, with no earlier significant bin of the same sign. Intensifying and diminishing patterns show significant directional change within a long-standing hot/cold concentration. Historical patterns lose their significant terminal status after a high share of earlier significant bins. Oscillating patterns include an earlier opposite-sign episode and a significant final bin. Sporadic patterns recur intermittently, end in a significant same-sign bin and contain no opposite-sign episode. The explicit precedence is new, long-standing, consecutive, oscillating and sporadic. These rules summarise observed sequences rather than predict future conflict. Automated tests cover both signs, the 90% boundary and non-significant final months.

6.4.1 Event counts: Consecutive cold spot
This pattern covers 1 townships; the largest regional counts are Shan (North) (1). A previously absent same-sign pattern forms an uninterrupted cold run at the end of the study. Its persistence beyond September 2025 is unknown. Of these townships, 1 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 1 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.


6.4.2 Event counts: Intensifying cold spot
This pattern covers 2 townships; the largest regional counts are Shan (East) (1) and Shan (North) (1). At least 90% of months are cold and the Gi* trend becomes more negative. This is strengthening low-value clustering, not intensifying violence. Of these townships, 2 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 2 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.


6.4.3 Event counts: Oscillating hot spot
This pattern covers 17 townships; the largest regional counts are Magway (4) and Tanintharyi (4). The terminal hot episode follows an earlier cold episode. This changing sign argues against describing the entire period as uniformly high-conflict. Of these townships, 10 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 15 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.


6.4.4 Event counts: Sporadic cold spot
This pattern covers 34 townships; the largest regional counts are Yangon (20) and Shan (South) (6). Low-value clustering recurs intermittently and the final month is cold relative to the pooled reference. This is neither proof of safety nor necessarily a decline in absolute events. Of these townships, 22 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 32 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.


6.4.5 Event counts: Sporadic hot spot
This pattern covers 6 townships; the largest regional counts are Kayin (2) and Shan (North) (2). High-value episodes recur intermittently and the final month is hot. This supports a terminal concentration, but not sustained intensification throughout the study. Of these townships, 5 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 6 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.


6.4.6 Reported fatalities: Intensifying cold spot
This pattern covers 2 townships; the largest regional counts are Ayeyarwady (1) and Yangon (1). At least 90% of months are cold and the Gi* trend becomes more negative. This is strengthening low-value clustering, not intensifying violence. Of these townships, 1 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 2 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.


6.4.7 Reported fatalities: Oscillating cold spot
This pattern covers 1 townships; the largest regional counts are Shan (North) (1). The terminal cold episode follows earlier hot clustering. This indicates a change in relative concentration, not demonstrated conflict resolution. Of these townships, 1 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 1 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.


6.4.8 Reported fatalities: Oscillating hot spot
This pattern covers 6 townships; the largest regional counts are Kachin (1) and Magway (1). The terminal hot episode follows an earlier cold episode. This changing sign argues against describing the entire period as uniformly high-conflict. Of these townships, 4 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 6 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.


6.4.9 Reported fatalities: Sporadic cold spot
This pattern covers 43 townships; the largest regional counts are Yangon (30) and Ayeyarwady (5). Low-value clustering recurs intermittently and the final month is cold relative to the pooled reference. This is neither proof of safety nor necessarily a decline in absolute events. Of these townships, 38 also pass the three-month-block trend check and 40 survive BH adjustment of the Mann-Kendall tests. The pattern is descriptive and its nominal trend significance should not override these uncertainty checks.

This pattern covers 6 townships; the largest regional counts are Rakhine (2) and Tanintharyi (2). High-value episodes recur intermittently and the final month is hot. section: 8.2 Conditional spatial random-labelling of fatality severity
text:
8.2 Conditional spatial random-labelling of fatality severity
Additional question: Which local neighbourhoods have more reported fatalities than expected from their recorded event locations, months and event-type composition?
This extends the core count-based analyses through a conditional simulation. Each event keeps its township, month and type. Within each month-by-event-type stratum, fatality marks are randomly reassigned among the recorded events without replacement. The procedure preserves incident frequency, temporal patterns, type composition and each stratum’s entire fatality distribution. It breaks the association between location and severity within those strata.
The reference model adapts the grouped random-labelling principle documented in spatstat’s rlabel: locations stay fixed while marks are permuted within groups. Here, explicit R code computes an areal-neighbourhood statistic rather than a point-pattern summary function.
The statistic for each township is the fatality sum in its self-including queen neighbourhood. Its conditional expectation sums the month/type mean fatality mark over the events in that neighbourhood. The observed-to-expected ratio describes excess severity, not individual fatality risk. A one-sided upper-tail p-value uses 999 randomisations and a plus-one correction. BH adjusts the family of 330 township neighbourhoods. The complete analysis is repeated on precision-code-1 records, with expectations recalculated for that subset.
This is a random-labelling reference model, not a causal model. It assumes exchangeable fatality marks within each month/type stratum under the null. Reporting differences, actor composition and correlated incidents can violate that assumption. Overlapping neighbourhoods are dependent; the BH screen is exploratory and does not establish arbitrary-dependence control. The same underlying incidents can contribute to several neighbourhoods, so their totals must never be added together. The approach complements raw fatality hotspots by conditioning on recorded frequency and type.






Figure 15: Excess neighbourhood fatality severity under conditional random labelling.



53 neighbourhoods have excess fatality marks at BH q < 0.05; 21 also pass the independently rerun precision-code-1 analysis. Among full-data excess neighbourhoods, 32 are outside the ordinary fatality Gi* hotspot set after BH adjustment. These findings answer a conditional severity question that the raw-count maps do not. Examples with the largest observed-to-expected ratios include Kyangin (Ayeyarwady); Myanaung (Ayeyarwady); Padaung (Bago (West)). Each name identifies the focal township plus its neighbours. The result supports checking local incident composition and reporting before interpreting fatalities simply as a consequence of frequent events. Of these three examples, 0 retain q < 0.05 in the precise-only analysis, so the large ratios alone should not determine which places receive strongest emphasis.

8.3.1 S1: Kyunhla neighbourhood
Across 9 townships, 1,830 retained incidents contain 4,929 reported fatalities against a conditional expectation of 3221.0. The O/E ratio is 1.53 (BH q = 0.013), increasing to 1.75 in the precision-code-1 analysis (q = 0.019). Battles contribute 1082.7 excess fatalities, or 63.4% of the net excess; 2022 supplies the largest calendar-period contribution. The single largest incident represents 3.6% of observed fatalities, while the largest month contributes 6.3%. These concentration checks describe leverage but do not replace a leave-one-out test. The focal township is not an ordinary BH-adjusted event or fatality hotspot. The added insight is therefore conditional severity beyond raw concentration. This supports checking incident composition and reporting in the neighbourhood, not a causal explanation or an assistance ranking.

10.1 A constant-share comparison
Raw-count EHSA uses a pooled space-time reference and can respond to nationwide change. The following diagnostic asks whether the four township profiles also gain or lose share of the recorded national total. For township i and period t, the share is its retained count divided by the sum across all 330 townships. The benchmark for January-September 2025 holds the township’s January-September 2024 share constant and multiplies it by the 2025 national total. Relative growth is (local 2025 / local 2024) / (national 2025 / national 2024); values above one indicate a share gain. A zero starting local total leaves that ratio undefined rather than introducing a pseudocount.
This is an accounting benchmark, not a fitted causal model, population-adjusted risk estimate or replacement EHSA. Shares are compositional and use the same potentially incomplete reporting system. Comparing the same nine months reduces unequal-duration and calendar-season differences, but cannot remove changes in reporting coverage. Quarterly shares below use all three months’ totals, not an average of monthly percentages.

National retained events fall from 9,975 to 8,749 between January-September 2024 and 2025 (12.3%). In contrast, Kawkareik’s events increase from 122 to 356 and its share rises from 1.22% to 4.07%; Nawnghkio increases from 202 to 341, with its share rising from 2.03% to 3.90%. Their matched-window increases therefore cannot be explained by an increasing national event total in that window. Monywa and Myingyan lose event share as well as counts. These comparisons strengthen the geographical interpretation while leaving the original full-period EHSA tests unchanged.






Figure 25: Quarterly fatality shares of the national total.



National reported fatalities decline by 29.5% in the matched windows. Kawkareik increases in both count and share. Nawnghkio’s count falls from 91 to 70, yet its national share rises slightly from 0.54% to 0.59%; Myingyan similarly falls from 428 to 313 while its share moves from 2.54% to 2.63%. Neither small share increase establishes a statistically significant increase. Monywa declines in both measures. Absolute decline and relative concentration can coexist, so a falling fatality count alone does not establish improvement relative to the national pattern.
The strongest supported statement is window-specific: Kawkareik and Nawnghkio gain event share during a national decline, while Monywa and Myingyan lose event share. This diagnostic does not show that national trends have been removed from all 57-month Gi* trajectories. Causal explanations and independent reporting validation remain outside the available evidence.

title: Conflict patterns across Myanmar townships
text:
10.2 Contemporaneous humanitarian context
Nawnghkio, northern Shan. OCHA’s 28 March 2025 update, “Continued insecurity in the Northeast” describes repeated clashes and aerial attacks in Nawnghkio, including reported civilian casualties. This supplies contemporaneous context for examining its growing event share. It does not independently verify this report’s exact incident counts or explain why fatalities decline in the matched window. Humanitarian reporting and ACLED may also draw on overlapping underlying sources.
Kawkareik within Kayin. The same OCHA update, southeastern Myanmar discussion reports approximately 2,800 people displaced in Kayin since mid-February 2025, alongside conflict-related needs for food, medicine and relief items. This evidence is at state level, not an estimate for Kawkareik. It supports examining displacement and service access alongside the township’s increased recorded activity, but cannot allocate those displaced people to this case or establish a township-level causal explanation.
Implication for both cases. OCHA’s 23 September 2025 update identifies continued displacement and severe humanitarian-access constraints, particularly in the Northwest and Southeast. Accordingly, neither a national decline in recorded counts nor a local cold-spot label establishes falling humanitarian need. These sources fall within the study period. They are contextual evidence, not extra observations inserted into the statistical tests, and do not validate the selected Sagaing severity neighbourhoods’ 2022–2023 peaks.

title: Conflict patterns across Myanmar townships
text:
Preparation code
 # Prepare a complete township-month panel without changing the raw files.
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(sf);library(dplyr);library(tidyr);library(readr);library(lubridate);library(spdep)})
dir.create('outputs',showWarnings=FALSE)
set.seed(20261018)
raw_paths <- c('data/Aspatial/ACLED_Data_Myanmar_Jan2021-Sep2025.csv', list.files('data/Geospatial',full.names=TRUE))
raw_hashes <- tools::md5sum(raw_paths)
raw <- read_csv(raw_paths[1],show_col_types=FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(raw$event_id_cnty))
raw$event_date <- as.Date(raw$event_date)
stopifnot(!anyNA(raw$event_date), all(raw$fatalities>=0), !anyNA(raw$fatalities))
event_types <- c('Battles','Explosions/Remote violence','Violence against civilians')
eligible <- raw %>% filter(country=='Myanmar',event_date>=as.Date('2021-01-01'),event_date<=as.Date('2025-09-30'),event_type %in% event_types)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(eligible$longitude)),all(is.finite(eligible$latitude)))
townships_raw <- st_read('data/Geospatial/mmr_polbnda_adm3_250k_mimu_1.shp',quiet=TRUE)
stopifnot(nrow(townships_raw)==330,all(as.character(townships_raw$PCode_V)=='9.4'),!anyDuplicated(townships_raw$TS_PCODE))
invalid_before <- sum(!st_is_valid(townships_raw))
crs_area <- '+proj=aea +lat_1=10 +lat_2=28 +lat_0=19 +lon_0=96 +datum=WGS84 +units=m +no_defs'
townships <- townships_raw %>% st_make_valid() %>% st_transform(crs_area) %>% arrange(TS_PCODE)
stopifnot(all(st_is_valid(townships)),!any(st_is_empty(townships)))
townships$area_km2 <- as.numeric(st_area(townships))/1e6
coords <- eligible %>% distinct(longitude,latitude)
pts <- st_as_sf(coords,coords=c('longitude','latitude'),crs=4326,remove=FALSE) %>% st_transform(st_crs(townships))
hits <- st_intersects(pts,townships)
coords$match_count <- lengths(hits)
coords$township_id <- vapply(hits,function(h) if(length(h)==1)townships$TS_PCODE[h] else NA_character_,character(1))
nearest <- st_nearest_feature(pts,townships)
coords$nearest_id <- townships$TS_PCODE[nearest]
coords$nearest_m <- as.numeric(st_distance(pts,townships[nearest,],by_element=TRUE))
events <- eligible %>% left_join(coords,by=c('longitude','latitude')) %>% mutate(month=as.Date(format(event_date,'%Y-%m-01')))
assigned <- events %>% filter(!is.na(township_id))
unassigned <- events %>% filter(is.na(township_id))
months <- seq(as.Date('2021-01-01'),as.Date('2025-09-01'),by='month')
panel <- expand_grid(township_id=townships$TS_PCODE,month=months) %>%
 left_join(assigned %>% group_by(township_id,month) %>% summarise(events=n(),fatalities=sum(fatalities),.groups='drop'),by=c('township_id','month')) %>%
 mutate(across(c(events,fatalities),~replace_na(.x,0))) %>% arrange(month,township_id)
stopifnot(nrow(panel)==330*57,sum(panel$events)==nrow(assigned),sum(panel$fatalities)==sum(assigned$fatalities),!anyDuplicated(panel[c('township_id','month')]))
totals <- panel %>% group_by(township_id) %>% summarise(events=sum(events),fatalities=sum(fatalities),active_months=sum(events>0),.groups='drop')
townships <- townships %>% left_join(totals,by=c('TS_PCODE'='township_id'))
audit <- tibble(stage=c('Input rows','Outside Myanmar','Outside requested dates','Other event types within Myanmar/time','Eligible armed-conflict records','Unique spatially assigned records','Unassigned or ambiguous records','Assigned reported fatalities','Invalid polygons repaired','Townships','Months','Township-month bins'),
 value=c(nrow(raw),sum(raw$country!='Myanmar'),sum(raw$event_date<min(months)|raw$event_date>as.Date('2025-09-30')),sum(raw$country=='Myanmar' & !(raw$event_type %in% event_types)),nrow(events),nrow(assigned),nrow(unassigned),sum(assigned$fatalities),invalid_before,nrow(townships),length(months),nrow(panel)))
precision <- assigned %>% count(geo_precision,time_precision,name='records')
name_check <- assigned %>% left_join(st_drop_geometry(townships) %>% select(TS_PCODE,TS),by=c('township_id'='TS_PCODE')) %>% summarise(missing_admin3=sum(is.na(admin3)),exact_name_disagreement=sum(!is.na(admin3)&tolower(trimws(admin3))!=tolower(trimws(TS))))
quality <- list(audit=audit,precision=precision,name_check=name_check,
 unmatched=unassigned %>% count(geo_precision,match_count,name='records'),
 near_boundary=sum(unassigned$match_count==0 & unassigned$nearest_m<=1000),
 event_types=raw %>% count(event_type,name='records'), hashes=raw_hashes)
saveRDS(list(townships=townships,panel=panel,assigned=assigned,unassigned=unassigned,months=months,quality=quality), 'outputs/prepared.rds')
write_csv(audit,'outputs/data_audit.csv')
print(audit,n=Inf);print(quality$unmatched);print(name_check)
cat('Unassigned within 1 km:',quality$near_boundary,'\n')

title: Conflict patterns across Myanmar townships
text:
Statistical code
 # Local association and a one-month-lag space-time Gi* analysis.
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(spdep);library(Kendall);library(dplyr);library(tidyr);library(sf)})
d <- readRDS('outputs/prepared.rds')
g <- d$townships
n <- nrow(g); nt <- length(d$months)
set.seed(20261018)
spdep::set.coresOption(1L)
nb0 <- poly2nb(g,queen=TRUE,row.names=g$TS_PCODE,snap=10)
xy <- st_coordinates(st_point_on_surface(g))
isolates <- which(card(nb0)==0L)
nb <- nb0
if(length(isolates)) {
  kn <- knn2nb(knearneigh(xy,k=1))
  for(i in isolates) {j <- kn[[i]][1];nb[[i]]<-as.integer(j);nb[[j]]<-sort(unique(as.integer(c(nb[[j]][nb[[j]]>0],i))))}
}
lw <- nb2listw(nb,style='W',zero.policy=TRUE)
gstar_w <- nb2listw(include.self(nb),style='W',zero.policy=TRUE)
kn6 <- make.sym.nb(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy,k=6),row.names=g$TS_PCODE))
weights_audit <- data.frame(township=g$TS,code=g$TS_PCODE,queen_neighbours=card(nb0),analysis_neighbours=card(nb),isolate_link_added=seq_len(n)%in%isolates)
local_results <- function(x,w,star,seed=20261018,nsim=4999L) {
  mi <- localmoran_perm(x,w,nsim=nsim,alternative='two.sided',iseed=seed,no_repeat_in_row=TRUE,zero.policy=TRUE)
  gi <- localG_perm(x,star,nsim=nsim,alternative='two.sided',iseed=seed+1L,no_repeat_in_row=TRUE,zero.policy=TRUE)
  z <- as.numeric(scale(x)); lagz <- lag.listw(w,z,zero.policy=TRUE)
  pmi <- mi[,'Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim']; pgi <- attr(gi,'internals')[,'Pr(z != E(Gi)) Sim']
  tibble(Ii=mi[,'Ii'],moran_p=pmi,moran_q=p.adjust(pmi,'BH'),gi_z=as.numeric(gi),gi_p=pgi,gi_q=p.adjust(pgi,'BH'),
    lisa=ifelse(pmi<.05,ifelse(z>=0,ifelse(lagz>=0,'High-High','High-Low'),ifelse(lagz>=0,'Low-High','Low-Low')),'Not significant'),
    hotspot=ifelse(pgi<.05,ifelse(as.numeric(gi)>0,'Hot spot','Cold spot'),'Not significant'))
}
static <- bind_rows(lapply(c('events','fatalities'),function(v) bind_cols(tibble(code=g$TS_PCODE,variable=v),local_results(g[[v]],lw,gstar_w))))

# Time-major ordering: each monthly block contains the same 330 townships.
stnb <- vector('list',n*nt)
for(t in seq_len(nt)) for(i in seq_len(n)) {
  spatial <- sort(unique(c(i,nb[[i]][nb[[i]]>0])))
  here <- (t-1L)*n+i
  stnb[[here]] <- sort(as.integer(c((t-1L)*n+spatial,if(t>1L)(t-2L)*n+spatial else integer())))
}
class(stnb)<-'nb';attr(stnb,'region.id')<-as.character(seq_along(stnb));attr(stnb,'type')<-'space-time';attr(stnb,'sym')<-FALSE;attr(stnb,'self.included')<-TRUE
stw <- nb2listw(stnb,style='W',zero.policy=TRUE)
stopifnot(all(vapply(seq_along(stnb),function(i)i%in%stnb[[i]],logical(1))))

# Explicit, sign-specific pattern rules. No classification depends on place names.
classify_pattern <- function(z,p,tau,mkp) {
  hot<-p<.05 & z>0;cold<-p<.05 & z<0;m<-length(z)
  one_side <- function(a,opp,sign) {
    count<-sum(a);last<-a[m];share<-mean(a)
    if(count==0)return(NULL)
    if(last && count==1)return(paste('New',sign))
    if(share>=.9) {
      if(!last)return(paste('Historical',sign))
      if(mkp<.05) {
        growing <- if(sign=='hot spot') tau>0 else tau<0
        return(paste(if(growing)'Intensifying' else 'Diminishing',sign))
      }
      return(paste('Persistent',sign))
    }
    if(last) {
      run<-rle(rev(a))$lengths[1]
      if(run>=2 && run==count)return(paste('Consecutive',sign))
      if(any(opp))return(paste('Oscillating',sign))
    }
    # ArcGIS Pro 3.4 definitions require a same-sign significant final bin.
    if(last && !any(opp))return(paste('Sporadic',sign))
    NULL
  }
  a<-one_side(hot,cold,'hot spot');if(!is.null(a))return(a)
  a<-one_side(cold,hot,'cold spot');if(!is.null(a))return(a)
  'No pattern detected'
}
ehsa <- list(); gis <- list()
source('analysis/fast_gi.R')
for(v in c('events','fatalities')) {
  message('Space-time Gi*: ',v)
  x<-d$panel[[v]]
  gi<-fast_space_time_gi(x,stw,nsim=999L,seed=20261018L)
  zz<-gi$z; pp<-gi$p
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(zz)),all(is.finite(pp)),length(zz)==n*nt)
  gis[[v]]<-d$panel %>% select(township_id,month) %>% mutate(variable=v,gi_z=zz,p=pp,q=p.adjust(pp,'BH'))
  zm<-matrix(zz,nrow=n); pm<-matrix(pp,nrow=n)
  r<-lapply(seq_len(n),function(i) {
    mk<-MannKendall(zm[i,]); tau<-as.numeric(mk$tau); p<-as.numeric(mk$sl)
    if(!is.finite(p)){p<-1;tau<-0}
    # Three-month-block permutation preserves within-block temporal ordering.
    set.seed(20261018+i)
    blocks<-split(seq_len(nt),rep(seq_len(nt/3),each=3))
    obs<-tau
    null<-replicate(999,as.numeric(MannKendall(zm[i,unlist(blocks[sample(length(blocks))])])$tau))
    finite_null<-null[is.finite(null)]
    block_p<-if(length(finite_null)) (1+sum(abs(finite_null)>=abs(obs)))/(length(finite_null)+1) else 1
    tibble(code=g$TS_PCODE[i],variable=v,tau=tau,mk_p=p,block_p=block_p,hot_months=sum(pm[i,]<.05 & zm[i,]>0),cold_months=sum(pm[i,]<.05 & zm[i,]<0),
      final_gi=zm[i,nt],final_p=pm[i,nt],classification=classify_pattern(zm[i,],pm[i,],tau,p))
  })
  ehsa[[v]]<-bind_rows(r) %>% mutate(mk_q=p.adjust(mk_p,'BH'),map_class=ifelse(mk_p<.05 & classification!='No pattern detected',classification,'Not displayed'))
}
ehsa<-bind_rows(ehsa);gis<-bind_rows(gis)

# Sensitivity: alternative spatial neighbours, geolocation precision, and near-boundary records.
precise<-d$assigned %>% filter(geo_precision==1) %>% count(township_id)
x_precise<-replace_na(precise$n[match(g$TS_PCODE,precise$township_id)],0)
near<-d$unassigned %>% filter(match_count==0,nearest_m<=1000) %>% count(nearest_id)
x_near<-g$events+replace_na(near$n[match(g$TS_PCODE,near$nearest_id)],0)
sensitivity<-bind_rows(
 bind_cols(tibble(scenario='Six-nearest-neighbour graph',code=g$TS_PCODE),local_results(g$events,nb2listw(kn6,style='W'),nb2listw(include.self(kn6),style='W'))),
 bind_cols(tibble(scenario='Precisely located events only',code=g$TS_PCODE),local_results(x_precise,lw,gstar_w)),
 bind_cols(tibble(scenario='Add records within 1 km of boundary',code=g$TS_PCODE),local_results(x_near,lw,gstar_w)))
baseline<-static %>% filter(variable=='events')
sensitivity_summary<-sensitivity %>% group_by(scenario) %>% summarise(lisa_agreement=mean(lisa==baseline$lisa),hotspot_agreement=mean(hotspot==baseline$hotspot),hotspots=sum(hotspot=='Hot spot'),.groups='drop')
inference<-static %>% group_by(variable) %>% summarise(lisa_raw=sum(moran_p<.05),lisa_BH=sum(moran_q<.05),gi_raw=sum(gi_p<.05),gi_BH=sum(gi_q<.05),.groups='drop')
ehsa_summary<-ehsa %>% group_by(variable) %>% summarise(MK_raw=sum(mk_p<.05),MK_BH=sum(mk_q<.05),block_supported=sum(mk_p<.05 & block_p<.05),displayed=sum(map_class!='Not displayed'),.groups='drop')
saveRDS(list(static=static,ehsa=ehsa,gis=gis,weights=weights_audit,nb=nb,queen_components=n.comp.nb(nb0)$nc,analysis_components=n.comp.nb(nb)$nc,
 sensitivity=sensitivity,sensitivity_summary=sensitivity_summary,inference=inference,ehsa_summary=ehsa_summary), 'outputs/statistics.rds')
write.csv(static,'outputs/local_statistics.csv',row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(ehsa,'outputs/ehsa_statistics.csv',row.names=FALSE)
print(inference);print(ehsa_summary);print(sensitivity_summary)
print(table(ehsa$variable,ehsa$map_class))

Counts are not population-adjusted risks.')

text:
Supplementary global analysis code
analysis/09_global_moran.R adds global permutation tests, the scatterplot and the eight-setting sensitivity table without changing the original local, EHSA or robustness outputs. Its cache tracks the upstream signatures and its own source. Checks cover township alignment, the direct Moran formula, scatterplot slope, both Holm families, graph symmetry and repeated permutations. The earlier clean-directory verification below predates this stage.
 # Adapt the Hands-on 5(1) global test and 5(2) centred scatterplot workflow.
# Reuse the existing township order and repaired queen graph; do not change EHSA.
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(spdep);library(sf);library(dplyr);library(ggplot2)})
d <- readRDS('outputs/prepared.rds')
s <- readRDS('outputs/statistics.rds')
g <- d$townships
stopifnot(identical(as.character(attr(s$nb,'region.id')),as.character(g$TS_PCODE)),
          all(card(s$nb)>0))
w <- nb2listw(s$nb,style='W',zero.policy=FALSE)
n <- nrow(g)
B <- 9999L
rows <- points <- list()
tests <- list()
for(v in c('events','fatalities')) {
  x <- g[[v]]
  stopifnot(length(x)==n,all(is.finite(x)),sd(x)>0)
  z <- as.numeric(scale(x))
  lag_z <- lag.listw(w,z,zero.policy=FALSE)
  seed <- if(v=='events') 2026102101L else 2026102102L
  set.seed(seed)
  mc <- moran.mc(x,w,nsim=B,alternative='two.sided',zero.policy=FALSE)
  # Explicit inclusive tails with a +1 correction avoid a zero Monte Carlo p.
  simulated <- mc$res[seq_len(B)]
  observed <- as.numeric(mc$statistic)
  permutation_p <- min(1,2*min((1+sum(simulated>=observed))/(B+1),
                              (1+sum(simulated<=observed))/(B+1)))
  # Independent algebraic check: S0 = n for these non-isolated W weights.
  slope <- sum(z*lag_z)/sum(z*z)
  direct_I <- (n/Szero(w))*slope
  stopifnot(abs(Szero(w)-n)<1e-10,abs(direct_I-as.numeric(mc$statistic))<1e-12)
  local <- s$static %>% filter(variable==v)
  q <- local$moran_q[match(g$TS_PCODE,local$code)]
  quadrant <- case_when(z>0 & lag_z>0~'High-High',z<0 & lag_z<0~'Low-Low',
                        z>0 & lag_z<0~'High-Low',z<0 & lag_z>0~'Low-High',TRUE~'On mean')
  rows[[v]] <- data.frame(variable=v,n=n,I=direct_I,null_expectation=-1/(n-1),
                          permutation_p=permutation_p,permutations=B,seed=seed,slope=slope)
  points[[v]] <- data.frame(code=g$TS_PCODE,variable=v,z=z,lag_z=lag_z,
                            quadrant=quadrant,local_q=q,
                            local_support=ifelse(q<.05,'Local BH q < 0.05','Other townships'))
  tests[[v]] <- mc
}
results <- bind_rows(rows)
results$holm_p <- p.adjust(results$permutation_p,method='holm')
# Cross two representations with two graphs for each outcome. Keep all eight
# comparisons in one Holm family, including the original raw/queen results.
xy <- st_coordinates(st_point_on_surface(g))
kn6 <- make.sym.nb(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy,k=6),row.names=g$TS_PCODE))
graphs <- list(Queen=s$nb,`Symmetric 6-NN`=kn6)
sensitivity_rows <- list()
for(v in c('events','fatalities')) for(graph_name in names(graphs)) for(transform in c('Raw','log1p')) {
  x <- if(transform=='Raw') g[[v]] else log1p(g[[v]])
  sw <- nb2listw(graphs[[graph_name]],style='W',zero.policy=FALSE)
  base <- results[results$variable==v,]
  # The same seed within an outcome pairs the random reallocations across settings.
  set.seed(base$seed)
  mc <- moran.mc(x,sw,nsim=B,alternative='two.sided',zero.policy=FALSE)
  null <- mc$res[seq_len(B)]
  obs <- as.numeric(mc$statistic)
  pv <- min(1,2*min((1+sum(null>=obs))/(B+1),(1+sum(null<=obs))/(B+1)))
  centered <- x-mean(x)
  direct <- n/Szero(sw)*sum(centered*lag.listw(sw,centered))/sum(centered^2)
  stopifnot(abs(obs-direct)<1e-12)
  sensitivity_rows[[length(sensitivity_rows)+1L]] <- data.frame(variable=v,
    graph=graph_name,transform=transform,I=obs,permutation_p=pv,
    permutations=B,seed=base$seed,min_neighbours=min(card(graphs[[graph_name]])),
    max_neighbours=max(card(graphs[[graph_name]])))
}
sensitivity <- bind_rows(sensitivity_rows)
sensitivity$holm_p_8 <- p.adjust(sensitivity$permutation_p,'holm')
sensitivity$positive_supported <- sensitivity$I>0 & sensitivity$holm_p_8<.05
scatter <- bind_rows(points)
labels <- setNames(sprintf('%s\nGlobal I = %.3f',c('Event counts','Reported fatalities'),results$I),results$variable)
palette <- c('High-High'='#b2182b','Low-Low'='#2166ac','High-Low'='#ef8a62','Low-High'='#67a9cf','On mean'='#777777')
p <- ggplot(scatter,aes(z,lag_z))+
  geom_hline(yintercept=0,colour='grey65',linetype='dashed')+
  geom_vline(xintercept=0,colour='grey65',linetype='dashed')+
  geom_abline(data=results,aes(slope=slope,intercept=0),colour='#222222',linewidth=.65)+
  geom_point(aes(colour=quadrant,shape=local_support),size=2.3,alpha=.8)+
  facet_wrap(~variable,labeller=as_labeller(labels))+
  scale_colour_manual(values=palette)+
  scale_shape_manual(values=c('Local BH q < 0.05'=17,'Other townships'=1))+
  labs(title='Overall spatial association and local quadrants',
       subtitle='330 townships; January 2021 to September 2025; unchanged queen-based W weights',
       x='Standardised township total (z)',y='Spatial lag of the same z',colour='Descriptive quadrant',shape='Existing local Moran test',
       caption='Lines pass through the origin with slope I. Colour alone does not imply significance.\nTriangles use existing outcome-specific BH-adjusted local tests, not the global p-values.')+
  theme_minimal(base_size=12)+theme(legend.position='bottom',panel.grid.minor=element_blank(),
    plot.title=element_text(face='bold'),plot.caption=element_text(hjust=0))+
  guides(colour=guide_legend(nrow=1,order=1),shape=guide_legend(nrow=1,order=2))
dir.create('outputs/figures',recursive=TRUE,showWarnings=FALSE)
ggsave('outputs/figures/global_moran_scatter.png',p,width=11,height=7,dpi=160,bg='white')
saveRDS(list(results=results,scatter=scatter,tests=tests,sensitivity=sensitivity,
            sensitivity_graphs=graphs),'outputs/global_moran.rds')
write.csv(results,'outputs/global_moran_summary.csv',row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(sensitivity,'outputs/global_moran_sensitivity.csv',row.names=FALSE)
print(results)
print(sensitivity)

Extended analysis and verification
analysis/04_extensions.R implements temporal sensitivity, hotspot-set comparisons, the conditional severity test and deterministic case selection. analysis/05_extension_figures.R generates the corresponding figures. analysis/06_evidence_audit.R diagnoses name flags, recomputes static sensitivity results, calculates national-share benchmarks and decomposes supported severity cases. analysis/07_evidence_figures.R draws these additional results. analysis/08_severity_validation.R repeats the preselected severity cases across seeds and largest-record deletion scenarios, retaining full-family adjustment. The stage cache includes these scripts so changed analytical choices invalidate dependent outputs. analysis/test_analysis.R checks pattern boundaries, raw-data fingerprints, count reconciliation, map masks, name-audit accounting, national-share identities, additive severity decompositions, deletion accounting and a small-graph exhaustive comparison for the Gi* sampler. These internal tests complement, rather than replace, independent methodological review.
From the exercise directory, Rscript --vanilla analysis/test_analysis.R runs the checks after a build. Rscript --vanilla -e "Sys.setenv(TH02_REBUILD='1'); source('analysis/run_analysis.R')" rebuilds all stages. Required package versions and external spatial-library versions are recorded below; they document the tested environment rather than claiming compatibility with every package version. On Windows, Rcpp also requires a working Rtools toolchain. For non-ASCII temporary-path issues, set TMPDIR to an existing writable ASCII-only directory before starting R.
A separate-directory verification copied only source files and raw inputs before starting the complete analysis without any existing outputs or stage cache. Preparation, core statistics, extensions, evidence audits, severity validation and figure-data objects matched the project outputs at a numerical tolerance of 1e-12. Raw-input fingerprints matched and the automated checks passed. Both runs used the same installed R environment, so this verifies independence from cached results rather than portability to another machine or independent validation of the source data. To repeat the check, copy the required sources, styles and locally authorised data to an empty directory, run Rscript --vanilla analysis/run_analysis.R, then run the tests and render the report.

04_extensions.R
# Additional uncertainty checks and explanatory cases. Raw data are read only.
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(dplyr);library(tidyr);library(sf);library(spdep);library(Kendall)})
d <- readRDS('outputs/prepared.rds')
s <- readRDS('outputs/statistics.rds')
g <- d$townships
n <- nrow(g); nt <- length(d$months)
# Reuse the authoritative functions without executing the statistical pipeline.
for(expr in parse('analysis/02_statistics.R')) {
  if(is.call(expr) && identical(expr[[1]],as.name('<-')) && is.symbol(expr[[2]]) &&
     as.character(expr[[2]]) %in% c('classify_pattern','local_results')) eval(expr)
}
source('analysis/fast_gi.R')

sen_slope <- function(y) {
  ij <- combn(seq_along(y),2)
  median((y[ij[2,]]-y[ij[1,]])/(ij[2,]-ij[1,]))
}
mk_result <- function(y) {
  if(length(unique(y))<2L) return(c(tau=0,p=1))
  a <- Kendall::MannKendall(y)
  if(!is.finite(a$sl)) return(c(tau=0,p=1))
  c(tau=as.numeric(a$tau),p=as.numeric(a$sl))
}
block_test <- function(y,width,B=999L,seed=20261018L) {
  set.seed(seed)
  blocks <- split(seq_along(y),ceiling(seq_along(y)/width))
  observed <- mk_result(y)[['tau']]
  null <- replicate(B,mk_result(y[unlist(blocks[sample.int(length(blocks))])])[['tau']])
  (1+sum(abs(null)>=abs(observed)-1e-12))/(B+1)
}
space_time_weights <- function(nb,lag,n,nt) {
  out <- vector('list',n*nt)
  for(t in seq_len(nt)) for(i in seq_len(n)) {
    spatial <- sort(unique(c(i,nb[[i]][nb[[i]]>0])))
    out[[(t-1L)*n+i]] <- sort(as.integer(unlist(lapply(seq.int(max(1,t-lag),t),function(j)(j-1L)*n+spatial))))
  }
  class(out)<-'nb';attr(out,'region.id')<-as.character(seq_along(out))
  attr(out,'type')<-'space-time';attr(out,'sym')<-FALSE;attr(out,'self.included')<-TRUE
  nb2listw(out,style='W',zero.policy=TRUE)
}
summarise_cube <- function(z,p,variable,scenario) {
  zm<-matrix(z,nrow=n);pm<-matrix(p,nrow=n)
  bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(n),function(i){
    mk<-mk_result(zm[i,])
    cl<-classify_pattern(zm[i,],pm[i,],mk[['tau']],mk[['p']])
    tibble(code=g$TS_PCODE[i],variable=variable,scenario=scenario,
           tau=mk[['tau']],mk_p=mk[['p']],classification=cl,
           map_class=ifelse(mk[['p']]<.05 && cl!='No pattern detected',cl,'Not displayed'))
  }))
}

temporal <- list(); lag_results <- list(); bin_adjusted <- list(); slopes <- list()
for(v in c('events','fatalities')) {
  message('Trend robustness: ',v)
  gi<-s$gis %>% filter(variable==v)
  stopifnot(identical(gi$township_id,d$panel$township_id),identical(gi$month,d$panel$month))
  zm<-matrix(gi$gi_z,nrow=n);xm<-matrix(d$panel[[v]],nrow=n)
  baseline<-s$ehsa %>% filter(variable==v)
  temporal[[v]]<-bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(n),function(i){
    tibble(code=g$TS_PCODE[i],variable=v,block_3=baseline$block_p[i],
      block_6=block_test(zm[i,],6,seed=20262000L+i),
      block_12=block_test(zm[i,],12,seed=20263000L+i),
      lag1_acf=as.numeric(acf(zm[i,],plot=FALSE,lag.max=1)$acf[2]))
  }))
  slopes[[v]]<-tibble(code=g$TS_PCODE,variable=v,
    gi_slope=apply(zm,1,sen_slope),count_slope=apply(xm,1,sen_slope))
  bin_adjusted[[v]]<-summarise_cube(gi$gi_z,gi$q,v,'BH-adjusted space-time bins')
  for(lag in c(0L,2L)) {
    message('Alternative time neighbourhood: ',v,', lag ',lag)
    w<-space_time_weights(s$nb,lag,n,nt)
    result<-fast_space_time_gi(d$panel[[v]],w,nsim=999L,seed=20261018L)
    lag_results[[paste(v,lag)]]<-summarise_cube(result$z,result$p,v,paste0('Previous months: ',lag))
  }
}
temporal<-bind_rows(temporal);lag_results<-bind_rows(lag_results)
bin_adjusted<-bind_rows(bin_adjusted);slopes<-bind_rows(slopes)
checks<-s$ehsa %>% left_join(temporal,by=c('code','variable')) %>% left_join(slopes,by=c('code','variable')) %>%
  mutate(all_blocks=block_3<.05 & block_6<.05 & block_12<.05,
         trend_supported=mk_p<.05 & mk_q<.05 & all_blocks,
         evidence=case_when(map_class=='Not displayed'~'No displayed trend-pattern',
           trend_supported~'BH and all block checks',TRUE~'Sensitivity-dependent pattern'))
temporal_summary<-checks %>% group_by(variable) %>% summarise(nominal=sum(mk_p<.05),
  block_3=sum(mk_p<.05 & block_3<.05),block_6=sum(mk_p<.05 & block_6<.05),
  block_12=sum(mk_p<.05 & block_12<.05),BH_and_all_blocks=sum(trend_supported),
  displayed=sum(map_class!='Not displayed'),supported_displayed=sum(map_class!='Not displayed' & trend_supported),.groups='drop')

comparison<-bind_rows(lag_results,bin_adjusted) %>%
  left_join(s$ehsa %>% select(code,variable,baseline_class=classification,baseline_map=map_class),by=c('code','variable'))
scenario_summary<-comparison %>% group_by(variable,scenario) %>% summarise(
  class_agreement=mean(classification==baseline_class),
  displayed=sum(map_class!='Not displayed'),
  retained_same_pattern=sum(map_class==baseline_map & baseline_map!='Not displayed'),
  baseline_displayed=sum(baseline_map!='Not displayed'),.groups='drop')

# Extend the original spatial sensitivity checks to the second outcome.
xy<-st_coordinates(st_point_on_surface(g));kn6<-make.sym.nb(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy,k=6)))
lw<-nb2listw(s$nb,style='W',zero.policy=TRUE);star<-nb2listw(include.self(s$nb),style='W',zero.policy=TRUE)
precise<-d$assigned %>% filter(geo_precision==1) %>% group_by(township_id) %>% summarise(fatalities=sum(fatalities),.groups='drop')
near<-d$unassigned %>% filter(match_count==0,nearest_m<=1000) %>% group_by(nearest_id) %>% summarise(fatalities=sum(fatalities),.groups='drop')
sens_fatalities<-bind_rows(
 bind_cols(tibble(scenario='Six-nearest-neighbour graph',code=g$TS_PCODE),local_results(g$fatalities,nb2listw(kn6,style='W'),nb2listw(include.self(kn6),style='W'))),
 bind_cols(tibble(scenario='Precisely located events only',code=g$TS_PCODE),local_results(replace_na(precise$fatalities[match(g$TS_PCODE,precise$township_id)],0),lw,star)),
 bind_cols(tibble(scenario='Add records within 1 km of boundary',code=g$TS_PCODE),local_results(g$fatalities+replace_na(near$fatalities[match(g$TS_PCODE,near$nearest_id)],0),lw,star)))
spatial<-bind_rows(mutate(s$sensitivity,variable='events'),mutate(sens_fatalities,variable='fatalities')) %>%
 left_join(s$static %>% select(code,variable,baseline_hotspot=hotspot),by=c('code','variable'))
spatial_summary<-spatial %>% group_by(variable,scenario) %>% summarise(
 baseline_hot=sum(baseline_hotspot=='Hot spot'),alternative_hot=sum(hotspot=='Hot spot'),
 retained=sum(hotspot=='Hot spot' & baseline_hotspot=='Hot spot'),
 gained=sum(hotspot=='Hot spot' & baseline_hotspot!='Hot spot'),
 lost=sum(hotspot!='Hot spot' & baseline_hotspot=='Hot spot'),
 Jaccard=sum(hotspot=='Hot spot' & baseline_hotspot=='Hot spot')/sum(hotspot=='Hot spot' | baseline_hotspot=='Hot spot'),.groups='drop')

# Value-added question: where do frequency and fatality concentration disagree?
# Use separately BH-adjusted Gi* families. No ranking of individual risk is implied.
ev<-s$static %>% filter(variable=='events') %>% select(code,event_z=gi_z,event_q=gi_q)
fa<-s$static %>% filter(variable=='fatalities') %>% select(code,fatality_z=gi_z,fatality_q=gi_q)
concordance<-inner_join(ev,fa,by='code') %>%
 mutate(event_hot=event_z>0 & event_q<.05,fatality_hot=fatality_z>0 & fatality_q<.05,
  category=case_when(event_hot & fatality_hot~'Both outcomes',event_hot~'Events only',fatality_hot~'Fatalities only',TRUE~'Neither outcome')) %>%
 left_join(st_drop_geometry(g) %>% select(code=TS_PCODE,township=TS,region=ST,events,fatalities),by='code')
concordance_summary<-concordance %>% group_by(category) %>% summarise(townships=n(),events=sum(events),fatalities=sum(fatalities),.groups='drop')
joint_stability<-spatial %>% mutate(hot=gi_z>0 & gi_q<.05) %>% select(code,variable,scenario,hot) %>%
 pivot_wider(names_from=variable,values_from=hot) %>%
 left_join(concordance %>% select(code,baseline_both=category),by='code') %>% group_by(scenario) %>%
 summarise(both=sum(events & fatalities),retained_baseline_both=sum(events & fatalities & baseline_both=='Both outcomes'),.groups='drop')

# Conditional spatial random-labelling test of incident severity.
# Hold incident locations, months and types fixed. Shuffle fatality marks only
# within month x event-type strata, preserving each stratum's fatality distribution.
# The self-including queen graph aggregates marks into local neighbourhoods.
severity_test <- function(records,scenario,B=999L,seed=20264000L) {
  idx<-match(records$township_id,g$TS_PCODE)
  aggregate_town<-function(x) as.numeric(rowsum(c(x,rep(0,n)),c(idx,seq_len(n)),reorder=TRUE))
  strata<-split(seq_len(nrow(records)),interaction(records$month,records$event_type,drop=TRUE))
  marks<-records$fatalities
  expected_marks<-marks
  for(ids in strata) expected_marks[ids]<-mean(marks[ids])
  adjacency<-nb2mat(include.self(s$nb),style='B',zero.policy=TRUE)
  observed<-as.numeric(adjacency %*% aggregate_town(marks))
  expected<-as.numeric(adjacency %*% aggregate_town(expected_marks))
  upper<-integer(n)
  set.seed(seed)
  for(b in seq_len(B)) {
    shuffled<-marks
    for(ids in strata) shuffled[ids]<-marks[ids[sample.int(length(ids))]]
    simulated<-as.numeric(adjacency %*% aggregate_town(shuffled))
    upper<-upper+as.integer(simulated>=observed)
  }
  p<-(upper+1)/(B+1)
  tibble(code=g$TS_PCODE,scenario=scenario,neighbourhood_events=as.numeric(adjacency %*% aggregate_town(rep(1,length(idx)))),

 key=normalise_name(TS),base_key=normalise_name(sub(' *\\(.*$','',TS)),region_key=normalise_name(ST))

 exact_match=!name_missing & tolower(trimws(admin3))==tolower(trimws(name)),
 name_flag=!exact_match,key=normalise_name(admin3),region_key=normalise_name(admin1))
candidate_code<-function(key,region_key) {
 if(is.na(key)||key=='')return(NA_character_)
 hit<-which(lookup$key==key & lookup$region_key==region_key)
 if(length(hit)==0L)hit<-which(lookup$base_key==key & lookup$region_key==region_key)
 if(length(hit)==1L)lookup$code[hit] else NA_character_
}

 name_missing~'Missing township name',exact_match~'Exact name match',
 key==normalise_name(name)~'Formatting-only difference',
 candidate==township_id~'Boundary primary-name match',
 !is.na(candidate) & candidate!=township_id~'Conflicting unique township label',
 TRUE~'Unresolved name'))

# A Jaccard ceiling prevents selecting nearly identical neighbourhoods.
pool<-e$severity %>% filter(excess,precise_excess) %>% mutate(minimum_ratio=pmin(ratio,precise_ratio)) %>%

}

# Validate the previously selected cases without selecting replacement examples.
# Every randomisation and deletion scenario retains the full 330-test BH family.
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(dplyr);library(sf);library(spdep)})
d<-readRDS('outputs/prepared.rds');s<-readRDS('outputs/statistics.rds')
h<-readRDS('outputs/evidence_audit.rds')
g<-d$townships;n<-nrow(g)
for(expr in parse('analysis/04_extensions.R')) {
 if(is.call(expr) && identical(expr[[1]],as.name('<-')) && is.symbol(expr[[2]]) &&
    as.character(expr[[2]])=='severity_test')eval(expr)
}
seeds<-c(20265001L,20265002L,20265003L)
B<-1999L
samples<-list('All assigned events'=d$assigned,
 'Precision code 1'=filter(d$assigned,geo_precision==1))
repeated<-list();deleted<-list();deletion_audit<-list()
for(sample_name in names(samples)){
 records<-samples[[sample_name]]
 for(seed in seeds){
  message('Severity seed check: ',sample_name,', seed ',seed)
  out<-severity_test(records,sample_name,B=B,seed=seed)
  repeated[[paste(sample_name,seed)]]<-out %>% mutate(seed=seed,
   supported=q<.05 & observed>expected)
 }
 for(code in h$robust_cases$code){
  ids<-sort(unique(c(match(code,g$TS_PCODE),s$nb[[match(code,g$TS_PCODE)]])))
  candidates<-records %>% filter(township_id%in%g$TS_PCODE[ids]) %>%
   arrange(desc(fatalities),event_id_cnty)
  stopifnot(nrow(candidates)>0,candidates$fatalities[1]>0)
  # Remove one record, using its ID only in memory to break tied maxima.
  reduced<-records %>% filter(event_id_cnty!=candidates$event_id_cnty[1])
  stopifnot(nrow(reduced)==nrow(records)-1L)
  message('Largest-incident deletion: ',sample_name,', focal code ',code)
  out<-severity_test(reduced,sample_name,B=B,seed=seeds[1])
  deleted[[paste(sample_name,code)]]<-out %>% mutate(deletion_case=.env$code,
   supported=q<.05 & observed>expected)
  deletion_audit[[paste(sample_name,code)]]<-tibble(scenario=sample_name,
   deletion_case=code,removed_records=1L,removed_fatalities=candidates$fatalities[1],
   before_records=nrow(records),after_records=nrow(reduced),
   before_fatalities=sum(records$fatalities),after_fatalities=sum(reduced$fatalities))
 }
}
repeated<-bind_rows(repeated);deleted<-bind_rows(deleted)
deletion_audit<-bind_rows(deletion_audit)
cases<-h$robust_cases %>% select(code,township,region)
seed_cases<-repeated %>% inner_join(cases,by='code') %>%
 group_by(code,township,scenario) %>% summarise(runs=n(),supported_runs=sum(supported),
 ratio=first(ratio),p_min=min(p),p_max=max(p),q_min=min(q),q_max=max(q),.groups='drop')
seed_families<-repeated %>% group_by(scenario,seed) %>% summarise(
 supported_neighbourhoods=sum(supported),.groups='drop')
deletion_cases<-deleted %>% filter(code==deletion_case) %>% inner_join(cases,by='code') %>%
 left_join(deletion_audit,by=c('scenario','deletion_case')) %>%
 select(code,township,scenario,observed,expected,ratio,p,q,supported,removed_fatalities)
stopifnot(nrow(seed_cases)==6,nrow(deletion_cases)==6,
 identical(unname(tools::md5sum(names(d$quality$hashes))),unname(d$quality$hashes)))
saveRDS(list(seeds=seeds,B=B,repeated=repeated,seed_cases=seed_cases,
 seed_families=seed_families,deleted=deleted,deletion_cases=deletion_cases,
 deletion_audit=deletion_audit),'outputs/severity_validation.rds')

title: Conflict patterns in Myanmar
text:
Study question and data
Where does recorded conflict cluster, and where does clustering change over time?

330 townships, MIMU v9.4 boundaries.
57 months, January 2021 to September 2025.
53,992 assigned events, 89,220 reported fatalities.
Battles, explosions/remote violence and violence against civilians.

Methods: Global Moran’s I uses 9,999 permutations, local tests 4,999 and space-time Gi* 999, followed by Mann-Kendall trends.
Overall association: I = 0.490 for events and 0.558 for fatalities. Both pass the two-test Holm threshold (p = 0.0004).
Main maps show p < 0.05. Data-quality alternatives leave adjusted static hotspot sets unchanged.

title: Conflict patterns in Myanmar
text:
Recorded burden through time

Peak event month: November 2023, with 1,473 events. The 2025 series ends in September.

title: Conflict patterns in Myanmar
text:
Event-count clusters and outliers




37 High-High townships
2 spatial outliers
High-High means a high recorded total surrounded by high totals. An outlier differs from its neighbours.
Grey areas are not significant under this test. They are not established safe areas.
Sagaing contains 18 of 37 High-High townships under the Local Moran test shown here.

title: Conflict patterns in Myanmar
text:
Reported-fatality concentrations




43 nominal hot spots
33 overlap with event-count hot spots
Fatality totals complement event frequency but can be dominated by severe incidents. Recorded fatalities are estimates, not a verified death toll.

title: Conflict patterns in Myanmar
text:
Emerging event-count patterns




60 displayed township patterns
Colour requires a recognised hot/cold pattern and Mann-Kendall p < 0.05.
The time neighbourhood includes the current and previous month. Sporadic patterns require a significant final month under the cited Pro 3.4 definitions.
Hot patterns are mainly 6 sporadic and 17 oscillating townships.

January-September comparisons: national events decline 12.3%, while Kawkareik and Nawnghkio gain both events and national share. Monywa and Myingyan lose event share.
Fatality counts can fall while shares rise: Nawnghkio falls from 91 to 70 fatalities, but its share rises from 0.54% to 0.59% during a larger national decline.
This descriptive benchmark complements the report’s four profiles. It does not remove national trends from the full-period EHSA or estimate population risk.

title: Conflict patterns in Myanmar
section: Robustness changes the strength of evidence
text:
Robustness changes the strength of evidence










Outcome
Displayed trend-patterns
Also pass BH and all block checks




events
60

fatalities

23





Additional temporal support requires MK BH q < 0.05 and all 3-, 6- and 12-month block p-values < 0.05. Long-block resolution is limited.
BH-adjusted space-time bins leave 22 event and 0 fatality patterns displayed.
Global sensitivity: Positive Moran association survives 8/8 comparisons of raw/log1p totals and queen/symmetric six-neighbour weights (eight-test Holm p = 0.0016). This supports overall association, not the individual EHSA labels.
Overall concentration is stable across these checks. Temporal labels remain sensitive.

title: Conflict patterns in Myanmar
section: Fatality severity after conditioning on events
text:
Fatality severity after conditioning on events




53 baseline excess-severity neighbourhoods at BH q < 0.05. Three repeat seeds yield 50 to 58, so the total is simulation-sensitive.
21 also pass in the precise-location subset.
The simulation shuffles fatality marks within month and type while holding event locations fixed.
Kyunhla, Kawlin and Taze lie outside ordinary adjusted count hotspots. All 6 of 6 case/sample checks retain support across repeated seeds and after deleting each neighbourhood’s largest-fatality record.
Each new run uses 1,999 permutations and BH over all 330 neighbourhoods. Overlap, reporting bias and correlated incidents remain limitations.

title: Conflict patterns in Myanmar
text:
Peace-building implications and limits

Nawnghkio gains event share and passes the additional trend checks. Kawkareik also gains share, but its longer-block result requires caution.
Monywa illustrates why a grey EHSA area can still have a high accumulated burden.
Combine recorded conflict with displacement, access and service information before allocating assistance.
Treat low counts cautiously where reporting coverage may be weak.

The results support retrospective humanitarian discussion. They do not establish safe routes or operational targets.

title: In-class Exercise 7: Floating Catchment Area Accessibility
text:
This classroom exercise compares four floating catchment area approaches to eldercare accessibility in Singapore. It uses the supplied In-class_Ex07.zip data and adapts its R workflow, whose original document lists Xiaohan as author. The numerical model code is retained; the introductory text and website presentation have been expanded for this learning portfolio.
Demand is set to 100 for every hexagon and capacity to 100 for every facility. These are teaching assumptions, not measured elderly populations or service capacities. The resulting maps illustrate model behaviour rather than current service adequacy.


Extract the supplied archive into this exercise folder, keeping data/aspatial/OD_Matrix.csv and the complete shapefile components in data/geospatial. The spatial layers are Master Plan 2014 subzones, a prepared hexagonal grid, and eldercare locations. Use these matched inputs together rather than substituting newer layers independently. GIS metadata files ending in .qmd are not Quarto pages and are excluded from the website source folder.

title: Hands-on Exercise 8: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model
text:
How do distance and competition shape a store’s potential market area? This exercise follows Chapter 18 and applies the Huff model to the supplied Taichung teaching data. I prepare village population and store sales, construct an origin–destination distance matrix, map the patronage probability for store BT, and compare population-based allocations with recorded sales.
The model is an illustrative allocation among the supplied stores. It is not a calibrated forecast of current demand, revenue or profitability.

Spatial layers and coordinate reference systems
The supplied layers describe TWD97 / TM2 zone 121. Read their stored CRS definitions and transform them to EPSG:3826, a projected CRS in metres. Assigning a CRS label would not transform coordinates. Geometry checks precede distance calculation.

  st_transform(x, 3826) |> st_make_valid()

Aggregating and matching store sales
The sales table includes stores outside the spatial layer. Aggregate by store code, then match only the supplied study stores. Missing store identifiers and unmatched sales-store codes are counted, not treated as extra Taichung competitors. Sales amounts are not used as attractiveness, avoiding a circular comparison against the same sales observations later.

title: Hands-on Exercise 8: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model
text:
Supplement: alternative distance exponents
Compare \(\lambda=-1,-2,-3\) while keeping the origins, competitors and equal attractiveness fixed. This supplements the chapter and does not fit parameters to sales. Stronger distance decay concentrates probabilities on nearer stores. With equal attractiveness, the most probable store is the nearest one regardless of these negative exponents; uncertainty and total allocations can still change substantially.


Show code
scenarios <- lapply(c(-1, -2, -3), function(exponent) {
  result <- MCI::huff.shares(interaction_matrix, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD", "Store_size",
                             "distance", gamma = 1, lambda = exponent)
  as_tibble(result) |>
    mutate(VILLCODE = as.character(VILLCODE), Store_CD = as.character(Store_CD),
           lambda = exponent)
}) |> bind_rows()
scenario_origins <- scenarios |>
  group_by(lambda, VILLCODE) |>
  summarise(probability_sum = sum(p_ij), maximum_probability = max(p_ij),
            .groups = "drop")
stopifnot(max(abs(scenario_origins$probability_sum - 1)) < 1e-10)
scenario_totals <- scenarios |>
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(village) |> select(VILLCODE, P_CNT),
            by = "VILLCODE", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  group_by(lambda, Store_CD) |>
  summarise(allocated_population = sum(P_CNT * p_ij), .groups = "drop")
scenario_summary <- scenario_origins |>
  group_by(lambda) |>
  summarise(mean_maximum_probability = mean(maximum_probability), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(scenario_totals |> filter(Store_CD == "BT") |>
              select(lambda, BT_allocated_population = allocated_population), by = "lambda")

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Spatially Constrained Clustering
text: How does a requirement for geographically coherent regions change a multivariate classification? This exercise uses township ICT indicators to compare attribute-only clustering with a connected-region algorithm and a soft geographical penalty. It accompanies Chapter 12, with explicit checks for data alignment, feature scaling and cluster connectivity.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Spatially Constrained Clustering
text:
Household ownership rates
Counts are converted to ownership per 1,000 households. A township with many households should not automatically appear more digitally connected simply because it is larger. Rates use the same denominator within each township, but are not percentages and should not be added across devices.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6: Spatially Constrained Clustering
text:
Neighbour graph and edge costs


Show code
# Use planar topology explicitly for this historical polygon layer.
old_s2 <- sf_use_s2(FALSE)
nb <- poly2nb(shan, queen = TRUE, row.names = shan$TS_PCODE)
sf_use_s2(old_s2)
stopifnot(all(card(nb) > 0), n.comp.nb(nb)$nc == 1L)
costs <- nbcosts(nb, X)
cost_weights <- nb2listw(nb, glist = costs, style = "B")
tree <- mstree(cost_weights, ini = 1)
stopifnot(nrow(tree) == nrow(shan) - 1)
sk <- skater(tree[,1:2], data = X, ncuts = K - 1, method = "euclidean")
sk_groups <- sk$groups
table(sk_groups)


sk_groups
 1  2  3  4  5  6 
27 17  8  1  1  1 


Queen adjacency is the hard spatial constraint. Edge costs measure attribute differences, not kilometres. The spanning tree has 54 edges connecting 55 townships. Five cuts create six groups. No minimum population or township count is imposed, so singleton regions are possible. Modern spdep accepts the neighbour graph derived directly from sf; converting to a legacy spatial class is unnecessary.


Show code
map_shan <- st_transform(shan, 32647)
coords <- st_coordinates(st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(map_shan)))
par(mfrow = c(1,2), mar = c(1,1,3,1))
plot(st_geometry(map_shan), border = "grey65", main = "Queen neighbours")
plot(nb, coords, add = TRUE, col = "#2166ac", points = FALSE)
plot(st_geometry(map_shan), border = "grey65", main = "Minimum spanning tree")
plot(tree, coords, add = TRUE, col = "#b2182b", cex.lab = .5, cex.circles = .003)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))








Figure 7: Queen graph and minimum spanning tree in a projected display.





The drawing uses points on polygon surfaces only to position graph nodes. The edges derive from shared boundaries and feature costs. EPSG:32647 provides a regional display, not a road-network model.

Sensitivity to feature scaling


Show code
coassignment_agreement <- function(a, b) {
  upper <- upper.tri(outer(a, a, "=="))
  mean((outer(a, a, "==") == outer(b, b, "=="))[upper])
}
raw_cut <- cutree(hclust(dist(X_raw), method = "ward.D2"), K)
z_cut <- cutree(hclust(dist(X_z), method = "ward.D2"), K)
data.frame(Comparison = c("Min-max versus raw", "Min-max versus z-score"),
           Pair_agreement = c(coassignment_agreement(ward_groups, raw_cut),
                              coassignment_agreement(ward_groups, z_cut))) |> kable(digits = 3)





Comparison
Pair_agreement




Min-max versus raw
0.789


Min-max versus z-score
0.991





This label-invariant agreement counts township pairs for which two classifications agree on being together or apart. It is not adjusted for chance and can be high because many pairs are separated. Scaling affects the feature weights, so disagreement is a substantive modelling issue rather than a software error.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5(1): Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text: This exercise accompanies Chapter 9. The question is whether neighbouring Hunan counties have similar GDP per capita in 2012. The analysis treats county boundaries as fixed and tests the arrangement of an attribute, rather than the locations of point events. Part 2 examines individual counties.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5(1): Global Spatial Autocorrelation

Packages
Install missing packages once in the R console before rendering. The document does not install software during a render.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5(1): Global Spatial Autocorrelation

Import and join
An explicit county key prevents an accidental join on unrelated columns. The checks require a unique match for every polygon and retain polygon order for the weights.

attributes <- read_csv("data/aspatial/Hunan_2012.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

          setequal(boundary$County, attributes$County),
          all(st_is_valid(boundary)), !any(st_is_empty(boundary)))
hunan <- left_join(boundary, select(attributes, County, GDPPC),
                   by = "County", relationship = "one-to-one")
stopifnot(identical(hunan$County, boundary$County),
          all(is.finite(hunan$GDPPC)), all(hunan$GDPPC > 0))

title: Hands-on Exercise 5(1): Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Analytical test
The null randomly assigns the observed GDPPC values to the fixed counties. The one-sided alternative tests positive spatial association. Exchangeability is an assumption, not proof that economic development is generated randomly.


Show code
moran_result <- moran.test(hunan$GDPPC, weights,
                           alternative = "greater", randomisation = TRUE)
moran_result



    Moran I test under randomisation

data:  hunan$GDPPC  
weights: weights    

Moran I statistic standard deviate = 4.7351, p-value = 1.095e-06
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Moran I statistic       Expectation          Variance 
      0.300749970      -0.011494253       0.004348351 


The observed I is 0.3007, compared with the randomisation expectation -0.0115. The analytical p-value is 1.09e-06. A positive value indicates a province-wide tendency for similar values to be adjacent; it does not locate individual clusters or identify a cause.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5(1): Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Monte Carlo test


Show code
set.seed(1234)
moran_sim <- moran.mc(hunan$GDPPC, weights, nsim = 999,
                      alternative = "greater")
moran_sim



    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  hunan$GDPPC 
weights: weights  
number of simulations + 1: 1000 

statistic = 0.30075, observed rank = 1000, p-value = 0.001
alternative hypothesis: greater




Show code
ggplot(data.frame(I = moran_sim$res[seq_len(999)]), aes(I)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "#4878a8", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = unname(moran_sim$statistic), colour = "#b2182b", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -1/87, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Moran's I under random reassignment", y = "Permutations")








Figure 2: Permutation distribution of Moran’s I; the red line marks the observed statistic.





The simulated reference contains only the 999 reassigned datasets; the observed value is excluded from the histogram. The permutation p-value is 0.001. With 999 permutations, tail probabilities have limited resolution. This test and the analytical test use the same data and weights, so agreement is not independent replication.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5(1): Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Moran scatterplot


Show code
z <- as.numeric(scale(hunan$GDPPC))
wz <- lag.listw(weights, z)
slope <- unname(coef(lm(wz ~ 0 + z))[1])
stopifnot(abs(slope - unname(moran_result$estimate[1])) < 1e-10)
ggplot(data.frame(z, wz), aes(z, wz)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(colour = "#2166ac", size = 2) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = slope, colour = "#b2182b") +
  labs(x = "Standardised GDPPC", y = "Spatial lag of standardised GDPPC")








Figure 3: Standardised GDPPC and its spatial lag using row-standardised queen weights.





The line through the origin has slope I because the weights sum to the number of counties. The lag is computed after standardising GDPPC; independently standardising the lag would change this slope relationship. Quadrants describe relative values, not local significance.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Pattern Analysis
text:
Following Chapter 6, I explore the locations and timing of MODIS active-fire detections during 2023. The analysis combines spatial data preparation, temporal summaries, space-time kernel density estimation (STKDE), bandwidth selection and the space-time K-function.
My questions are: when are detections most frequent, how does their geographical concentration change through the year, and what can the joint spatial and temporal pattern tell us? Satellite detections are observations of thermal anomalies, not necessarily distinct fires or confirmed forest fires.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Pattern Analysis
text:
Loading packages


Show code
library(sf)

  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "C") +

Monthly counts and maps
Counts include months with zero detections. A count measures observations recorded by the sensor; cloud cover, revisit frequency and repeated observations can influence it.

  complete(Month_num = 1:12, fill = list(n = 0)) |>
  mutate(Month = factor(month.abb[Month_num], levels = month.abb))
ggplot(monthly, aes(Month, n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#238b8d") +
  labs(title = "Monthly fire detections", x = NULL, y = "Detections")









The largest monthly total is in Oct, with 185 detections, or 24.9% of this study’s annual total.
